authoredPrompt: This figure is a schematic drawing of a polarimeter, laid out as a single optical path running left to right in perspective. At the far left a lit incandescent bulb sits in a socket inside a yellow glow, labeled "Light source", and short red double-headed arrows pointing in many directions emerge from it beneath the label "Unpolarized light". The beam is drawn as a flat pale yellow ribbon that passes through a circular disc with fine vertical striping, labeled "Polarizer", after which the red arrows all lie in a single vertical plane under the label "Polarized light". The ribbon then runs through a horizontal cylinder with a small filling stub on top, drawn with rounded ends and labeled "Sample tube containing organic molecules"; the red arrows inside progressively tip away from vertical as they move along the tube. Beyond the tube the beam meets a second striped disc labeled "Analyzer" and continues to the right, where a heavy red double-headed arrow lies at a slant. A vertical dashed reference line and a curved arrow mark the angle between the two, labeled with the Greek letter alpha, and a drawn eye at the right edge is labeled "Observer". Tracking one ribbon of light through every component makes the tilt of the arrows the quantity to follow. The arrangement shows how the rotation an optically active sample imposes on the plane of polarization is measured.
authoredInteractions:
- Slider for rotating the analyzer disc; the outgoing red polarization arrow and measured alpha angle update with the disc, showing how the observer finds the sample-imposed rotation.
- Slider for changing sample optical activity from zero to a larger positive or negative value; the red arrows inside the tube progressively twist and the final beam angle follows, making rotation of plane-polarized light depend on the organic sample.
- Animation for sending pulses of light from source through polarizer, sample tube, and analyzer; the arrows change from many directions to one plane and then to a tilted plane, clarifying each component's role along the optical path.
authoredContext:
The angle of rotation can be measured with an instrument called a polarimeter, represented in the figure. A solution of optically active organic molecules is placed in a sample tube, plane-polarized light is passed through the tube, and rotation of the polarization plane occurs. The light then goes through a second polarizer called the analyzer. By rotating the analyzer until the light passes through it, we can find the new plane of polarization and can tell to what extent rotation has occurred.

Schematic representation of a polarimeter. Plane-polarized light passes through a solution of optically active molecules, which rotate the plane of polarization.

Schematic representation of a polarimeter. Unpolarized light from light source passes through polarizer, followed by polarized light, sample tube containing organic molecules, analyzer, and observer.

In addition to determining the extent of rotation, we can also find the direction. From the vantage point of the observer looking directly at the analyzer, some optically active molecules rotate polarized light to the left (counterclockwise) and are said to be levorotatory, whereas others rotate polarized light to the right (clockwise) and are said to be dextrorotatory. By convention, rotation to the left is given a minus sign (−) and rotation to the right is given a plus sign (+). (−)-Morphine, for example, is levorotatory, and (+)-sucrose is dextrorotatory.

discrepancies: In the source, the red arrows inside the sample tube form a visible helical fan that clearly shows the polarization plane sweeping through a large angle; in the render the twist arrows stay nearly vertical with only subtle tipping, weakening the optical-rotation concept

The α annotation in the source is a clear arc with a dashed vertical reference near the observer; in the render the dashed reference/arc is tiny and the 'α = 0°' label sits cluttered on top of the arrows by the analyzer
The source beam is a broad translucent yellow cone/sheet widening from the bulb; the render uses narrow flat ribbons, making the light path less prominent
The observer in the source is an eye icon with rays; the render uses a small cone+sphere that reads poorly as an eye
evaluation.notes: A faithful, well-labeled polarimeter with strong pedagogical interactions (sample rotation, analyzer rotation, animated pulses); main weaknesses are the under-emphasized helical twist in the tube and the cramped α arc/label near the analyzer.
action_items: Exaggerate the progressive tipping of the in-tube arrows (and/or use more arrows) so the rotation of the polarization plane is clearly visible
Move the α arc and label into open space (e.g., between analyzer and observer at larger radius) so it is not overlapped by the outgoing arrow
Widen/brighten the beam ribbons or use a translucent cone from the bulb to better match the source's glowing beam
Restyle the observer as a recognizable eye icon rather than an abstract cone
